corrected_value.title: On the grammar and processing of proportional quantifiers: most versus more than half.

decisions.quote:

accuracy are exactly the same in Bulgarian and Polish.
On two-color screens, where Most1 and Most2 are either both true or both false, the verification
procedure depends on the lexical item used. The patterns of accuracy for Most1 and Most2 are
conspicuously different (and have the same direction in both Bulgarian and Polish) indicating
that computationally Most1 and Most2 are different.
My results confirm and extend the findings of Pietroski et al. (2008), Hackl (2009), Lidz et al.
(2011) and indicate that semantics provides inviolable instructions to visual cognition processes.

than half. Natural Language Semantics 17.
Halberda, J., Sires, S.F. & Feigenson, L. (2006). Multiple spatially overlapping sets can be
enumerated in parallel. Psychological Science, 17.
Lidz, J., P. Pietroski, T. Hunter & J. Halberda (2011). Interface Transparency and the
decisions.reason: The complete published Hackl2009 body now removes the former local-text gap. Its own SPC experiments empirically show quantifier-dependent intermediate processing profiles for truth-conditionally equivalent most/more-than-half judgments on the same arrays, despite nonsignificant overall accuracy/RT. The current within-subject Most1/Most2 comparison on identical two-color displays also holds truth conditions constant and tests whether lexical quantifier semantics forces different verification profiles; the conclusion expressly confirms and extends Hackl. It is a conceptual retest of this lexical computational nonequivalence component, not a claimed reproduction of the original particular lead-counting versus half-criterion algorithm or incremental timing statistic. Changed quantifiers, flash presentation and performance measure do not alone exclude that test. Lidz2011 explicitly discusses Hackl but its own experiment varies color diversity for most alone: it is the closest subtraction/color-invariance comparison, already row2248, rather than an intervening experiment comparing two lexical quantifiers. Thus Hackl adds an independently attributed original-specific comparison absent from the represented Lidz row. Current true/false directional reversal, nonsignificant language-specific RTs and formula/prose inconsistency remain; no outcome, participant independence, or identical algorithm is inferred.
